newsitem.title: USA: Streisand helps Clinton raise $4 million from stars.
newsitem.headline: Streisand helps Clinton raise $4 million from stars.

text.p: President Bill Clinton wrapped up a four-state Western campaign swing on Thursday night surrounded by Hollywood stars who paid more than $4 million to see him and hear Barbra Streisand sing.

Actresses Sharon Stone and Carrie Fisher as well as actor Richard Dreyfuss and Tom Hanks were among the celebrities who mingled at the cocktail reception, concert and dinner at the swanky Beverly Hills home of supermarket king Ron Burkle.

The evening, which included singing by Streisand, the Eagles and Chicago, poetry from Maya Angelou and a speech by Hanks, was the finale of a three-day campaign swing through the western United States.
Clinton came to California bearing gifts -- including $1.3 million in new federal money for education -- but left with more, having pulled in about $4.5 million at two fundraisers in the state.
Thursday's dinner was his biggest haul, accounting for $4 million of the total $5.5 million that he raised during the three-day trip, which also included stops in Missouri, Colorado and Arizona.
All of the money goes to the Democratic Party.
Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart said about 1,000 people attended Thursday's fundraiser, held at a lavish hilltop estate built by silent screen actor Harold Lloyd.

As with most Hollywood events, there was a strict pecking order: $1,000 bought entry only to cocktails in the garden, $5,000 brought access also to the concert, and $12,500 to a seated dinner as well.
"From the bottom of my heart, I thank you and I ask you to remember that there are still 54 more days before anybody can celebrate anything," Clinton told the contributors.

"What you have done tonight will make it possible for us to carry on that fight, not just in the race for the presidency but in all the others that embody the choice between building a bridge to the future and trying to build one to the past," he added.

With less than two months before the Nov. 5 election, Clinton holds a commanding lead of 15 to 20 percentage points nationwide over his Republican opponent Bob Dole. In California, a recent survey by an independent pollster put him ahead by 23 points.

There were a few sour notes for Clinton on Thursday, including protestors near the fundraiser with signs calling for campaign finance reform. One group showed a drawing that showed a cigar-smoking fat cat with the caption "Welcome to California, Mr. President."
Clinton was to return to fly back to Washington after the dinner, arriving on Friday morning.
